Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los romances
scenes.desc: El flamenco distingue una docena de palos (romances, tonás, siguiriyas, soleares, tangos, cantiñas, cantes de Levante, fandangos, cantes de Málaga, ida y vuelta, aflamencados e híbridos), cada uno con sus estilos y sus creadores. Los básicos, los más antiguos, empiezan por el romance, la canción española más vieja transmitida oralmente, que los gitanos hicieron suya: es el verdadero punto de origen del cante. También llamados corridos, son las únicas coplas con continuidad narrativa (historias románticas, caballerescas o moriscas) y se cantan a palo seco, sin acompañamiento; con guitarra toman el son de la soleá por bulerías. Washington Irving los oyó en 1829 como «tonadas rudas y sencillas». Hoy casi no se cantan. José Blas Vega grabó en 1971 en el Puerto de Santa María dieciséis romances primitivos de siete intérpretes, todos gitanos, y los dividió en los de flores y Blancaflor, los carolingios, los del Cid, los de Bernardo el Carpio y los moriscos, como el de Zaide; su parentesco con tonás, carceleras, deblas y martinetes es evidente.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.body: After Brian Epstein's death in 1967, The Beatles' business affairs became chaotic. facts.title: Early 1967 High Point
facts.body: At the beginning of 1967, The Rolling Stones were experiencing a peak in their career. They had achieved numerous number-one hits and completed a massive tour across the United States, performing in many stadiums, including a notable occasion where they shared the stage with James Brown. "En el 67 los Rolling Stones, yo creo que estaban en uno de los puntos más altos, habían conseguido un montón de números, uno, habían hecho esa enorme gina por Estados Unidos en las que habían llenado un montón de estadios, incluso habían coincidido con el grandísimo James Brown, una actuación."

facts.title: 1967 Drug Arrests
facts.body: Coinciding with the release of their album *Between the Buttons* in 1967, members of The Rolling Stones faced incarceration for a brief period due to drug possession and consumption. This event severely damaged their public popularity and marked the onset of a downturn in the band's fortunes. "los Rolling Stones acabaron encarcelados era un pequeño, durante un pequeño trozo de tiempo, por posesión y consumo de drogas, entonces hizo caer mucho su popularidad."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: End of Andrew Loog Oldham Era (1967)
facts.body: In late 1967, as a direct response to the commercial and critical failures of the early year, The Rolling Stones officially terminated their professional relationship with producer Andrew Loog Oldham. Oldham had been a pivotal figure in establishing their early importance and success. "se acabó oficialmente la etapa con André Olman, que fue el productor que los hizo tan importantes."

facts.title: Dismissal of Manager and Legal Battle (1967)
facts.body: Before the end of 1967, The Rolling Stones fired their manager, which ignited a substantial legal battle. "acaban despidiendo a su manaller, al enclenque era con el que acababan con un enorme litijo legal, con el que acababan perdiendo los derechos de toda su discografía anterior a 1967."

facts.title: Rock and Roll to Rock – The Transition Happened June 1, 1967 with Sgt. Pepper
facts.body: "Rock and roll" described a specific style of music that rose in the 1950s and reigned for about a dozen years, originating from rhythm and blues. On June 1, 1967, the Beatles released Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, and this marks the moment when rock and roll graduated from a trendy, disposable music for teenagers into a recognized modern art form taken as seriously as Beethoven, jazz, and Broadway. From that point on, "rock" (as distinct from "rock and roll") referred to anything descended from the sounds of the early-to-mid 1950s. "At first, rock and roll was this trendy, fattish, disposable, immature music for kids and teenagers that would no doubt soon fade away."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.name: Rock & Roll

facts.title: Accidental Guitar Incident and Stage Persona Birth (October 30-31, 1967)
facts.body: The day before The Stooges' first show, guitarist Ron Ashton painted Iggy's Hawaiian guitar, including the pickups, rendering it useless. Iggy took the guitar on stage anyway, then abandoned it, dancing "like a nut" as his pants began to fall down. When the audience reacted positively, believing it was part of the show, Iggy amplified his erratic behavior, which was the foundational moment for his punk rock stage persona. "And it was this event that set Iggy on the road to becoming the Godfather of Punk."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: FAME Studios Session Incident (January 1967)
facts.body: During her initial session at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, which yielded "I Never Loved a Man the Way I Love You," the recording environment became chaotic. Franklin's then-husband and manager, Ted White, became intoxicated and had two brass players fired, purportedly for making advances toward Aretha, leading to a physical altercation between White and the studio owner. As a result, Jerry Wexler pulled Aretha out, making it the only time she ever recorded at FAME studios, though they completed one pivotal song. "The fame session was immortal but also kind of a mess. Franklin's then husband and manager Ted White got drunk and had two brass players fired supposedly for coming on to Aretha."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.name: Aretha Franklin

facts.title: Queen of Soul Coronation (1967)
facts.body: The moniker "Queen of Soul" was bestowed upon Aretha Franklin at a 1967 concert at Chicago's Regal Theater. During a multi-act bill headlined by Franklin, local disc jockey Purvis Span, who considered himself an arbiter of blues and soul, held a theatrical coronation ceremony at the end of the show, placing an actual crown on her head and proclaiming her the Queen of Soul. "He placed an actual crown on Franklin's head, pronouncing her the Queen of Soul. The name stuck."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.body: Pink Floyd was a pioneer in quadraphonic live sound, utilizing a custom-made 4-channel PA system as early as 1967. facts.title: Band Formation (Late 1967)
facts.body: The Stooges were formed by James Osterberg (later Iggy Pop) and a group of "local degenerates" one night in Detroit, inspired by a bag of dope and a Three Stooges movie marathon on television. "One night, over a bag of dope and a three-stooge's movie marathon on television, he and a bunch of local degenerates decided to form a band that they called the Stooge's."

facts.title: First Show Guitar Malfunction (October 31, 1967)
facts.body: On the day of their inaugural performance, Iggy Pop's Hawaiian guitar was rendered useless because guitarist Ron Ashton had painted it, pickups included. Iggy's subsequent abandonment of the guitar and spontaneous, wild dancing, combined with his pants falling down, led to the birth of his legendary, audience-loved punk rock stage antics. "So when the Stooge's hit the stage, Iggy's guitar was completely useless because of the paint."

facts.title: Debut Performance (October 31, 1967)
facts.body: The band, initially called Iggy and the Psychedelic Stooges, made their debut on October 31, 1967, in Ann Arbor, Michigan. They were characterized by a loud, spontaneous, sloppy, fuzzy, arrogant, violent, angry, and powerful sound. "And on October 31, 1967, Iggy and the psychedelic studios made their debut in Ann Arbor, Michigan."

facts.title: Formation and Members (1967)
facts.body: The band was formed in 1967 by James Newell Osterberg (Iggy), brothers Ron and Scott Ashton, and Dave Alexander. Iggy, who was a known drummer in Ann Arbor, befriended Ron Ashton, leading to Scott joining, and then Dave Alexander, a high school dropout who had traveled the UK in search of the meaning of The Beatles. "These four guys decided to form a band with Iggy out front and on keyboards."

facts.title: Jim Morrison's Influence (1967)
facts.body: On October 20, 1967, Iggy attended a Doors show at the University of Michigan and was greatly inspired by Jim Morrison's drunken behavior and provocative interactions with the audience, which influenced Iggy's own stage persona. "Iggy was there and he was inspired by Jim Morrison's drunkenness in the way he provoked the audience."

facts.title: First Gig (Halloween 1967)
facts.body: The Stooges' debut performance was on Halloween 1967 at their headquarters on State Street in Ann Arbor, described as "weird." Iggy wore an aluminum foil wig and played a Hawaiian guitar tuned only to E, Scott played oil drums with ball-peen hammers, and Dave created reverb effects by banging on Ron's amplifier. Despite the unconventional and "awful" performance, both band and audience, being high, considered it a success. "Iggy wore a wig made of strands of aluminum foil and played a Hawaiian guitar with every string tune to E."

facts.title: Band Formation (Late 1967)
facts.body: The Stooges were formed by James Osterberg (later Iggy Pop) and a group of "local degenerates" one night in Detroit, inspired by a bag of dope and a Three Stooges movie marathon on television. "One night, over a bag of dope and a three-stooge's movie marathon on television, he and a bunch of local degenerates decided to form a band that they called the Stooge's."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1
facts.name: The Stooges

facts.title: Debut Performance (October 31, 1967)
facts.body: The band, initially called Iggy and the Psychedelic Stooges, made their debut on October 31, 1967, in Ann Arbor, Michigan. They were characterized by a loud, spontaneous, sloppy, fuzzy, arrogant, violent, angry, and powerful sound. "And on October 31, 1967, Iggy and the psychedelic studios made their debut in Ann Arbor, Michigan."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop
facts.name: The Stooges

facts.title: First Gig (Halloween 1967)
facts.body: The Stooges' debut performance was on Halloween 1967 at their headquarters on State Street in Ann Arbor, described as "weird." Iggy wore an aluminum foil wig and played a Hawaiian guitar tuned only to E, Scott played oil drums with ball-peen hammers, and Dave created reverb effects by banging on Ron's amplifier. Despite the unconventional and "awful" performance, both band and audience, being high, considered it a success. "Iggy wore a wig made of strands of aluminum foil and played a Hawaiian guitar with every string tune to E."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?
facts.name: The Stooges

facts.title: First Show Guitar Malfunction (October 31, 1967)
facts.body: On the day of their inaugural performance, Iggy Pop's Hawaiian guitar was rendered useless because guitarist Ron Ashton had painted it, pickups included. Iggy's subsequent abandonment of the guitar and spontaneous, wild dancing, combined with his pants falling down, led to the birth of his legendary, audience-loved punk rock stage antics. "So when the Stooge's hit the stage, Iggy's guitar was completely useless because of the paint."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1
facts.name: The Stooges

facts.title: Formation and Members (1967)
facts.body: The band was formed in 1967 by James Newell Osterberg (Iggy), brothers Ron and Scott Ashton, and Dave Alexander. Iggy, who was a known drummer in Ann Arbor, befriended Ron Ashton, leading to Scott joining, and then Dave Alexander, a high school dropout who had traveled the UK in search of the meaning of The Beatles. "These four guys decided to form a band with Iggy out front and on keyboards."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?
facts.name: The Stooges

facts.title: Jim Morrison's Influence (1967)
facts.body: On October 20, 1967, Iggy attended a Doors show at the University of Michigan and was greatly inspired by Jim Morrison's drunken behavior and provocative interactions with the audience, which influenced Iggy's own stage persona. "Iggy was there and he was inspired by Jim Morrison's drunkenness in the way he provoked the audience."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: Dolly Parton's career began closely linked with Porter Wagoner starting in 1967. facts.body: Released on June 1, 1967, this album marked a turning point in music history, designed as a cohesive artistic work to be experienced in its entirety and sequence, totaling 39 minutes and 36 seconds. facts.title: First Proper Rock and Roll Concept Album
facts.body: Issued on June 1, 1967, this album is considered the first proper Rock and Roll concept album. While it barely holds together conceptually, it is unified by a fictional band exploring life in post-war Britain, and its release opened the floodgates for other bands to create concept albums. "But the first proper Rock and Roll concept album was probably Sergeant Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club band, which was issued by the Beatles, of course, on June 1, 1967."

facts.title: European Theatrical Career (1967-1971)
facts.body: After arriving in New York City in 1967 at age 18 and performing with blues rock combo The Crow, Donna moved to Germany in 1968 to play Sheila in the Munich production of the musical *Hair*, singing the German version "Wassermann." Her relocation to Germany was likened to the impact Hamburg had on The Beatles or Berlin on David Bowie. She quickly became fluent in German and participated in German productions of *Godspell*, *Showboat*, and the rock musical *The Me Nobody Knows* (known as *Ichbien-Ich*), later singing for the Viennese folk opera after moving to Vienna in 1971. "The musical opened in Germany in October 1968. More important to Donna than the show was Germany itself. Relocating there did for the future Donna Summer what gigs in Hamburg had done for the young Beatles at the turn of the 60s, or what Berlin would do for David Bowie in the 1970s."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.title: Escalating Provocation and Lack of Political Clarity (1967-1969)
facts.body: From 1967 to 1969, Jim Morrison's personality became increasingly extreme and complex, marked by a rapid, progressive degeneration. His irreverent nature led to frequent police detentions for what were often absurd reasons, such as insulting officers, inciting trouble, or public nudity. At concerts, he delivered speeches specifically designed to provoke the audience. Despite his rebellious image, he never held a clear political ideology, unlike contemporaries like Jimi Hendrix, John Lennon, or Janis Joplin, whose provocations were tied to specific ideals. His statements often remained diffuse allegories about rebellion, freedom, and love, without committing to any concrete political stance. "Jim Morrison empezó en cadenar toda una serie de detenciones por la policía, por las razones más ridículas y necesarias."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.body: Released in 1965, this debut album was starkly different from mainstream rock and roll which focused on cars and girls; instead, it explored the gritty realities of New York City, including crime, weird sex, strange people, and drugs, which was considered too extreme at the time. Despite selling only about 30,000 copies between 1965 and 1970 and peaking at number 199 on the Billboard Top 200 album charts, its influence was immense, with producer Brian Eno famously stating that everyone who bought a copy started a band. "When their debut album arrived in 1965, rock and roll was largely about cars and girls and various escapists and fun topics. Not the velvet underground. They were from the gritty streets of New York City where there was crime, weird sex, strange people and drugs, lots and lots of drugs."

facts.body: Released in March 1967, this album featured Nico and was produced by Andy Warhol, famously sporting a banana on its cover. It is widely considered by many as the beginning of underground, alternative, and experimental music. Recording began in April 1966 at Scepter Studios in New York. The production was quick as most material was already composed from John Cale and Lou Reed's demos. Integrating Nico proved challenging, ultimately leading her to sing some songs due to Warhol's insistence. The album was finished by mid-1966 but delayed due to significant censorship over its strong lyrics about masochism, sexual themes, and drugs (including the song "Heroin"). An executive from Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer initially called it "shit," but ironically, his Verve Records division ultimately released it. Further delays were caused by Warhol's insistence on a peelable banana sticker for the cover, making production expensive and complex. Despite the delays, it was a massive commercial failure upon release, with no promotional support from the record label. "se considera por muchos el inicio de la música underground, posiblemente el inicio de la música alternativa, música experimental."

facts.body: In 1967, Charlie Pride became the second African American to be granted membership to the Grand Ole Opry, and the first since harmonica player DeFord Bailey, who last played at the Opry in 1941. This marked a significant milestone for racial integration in country music's premier institution. facts.body: Porter Wagoner gave Dolly Parton her start in the music industry, and her career was linked with his from 1967. She performed on his TV show and was part of his touring company, recording approximately 12 albums with him. Wagoner reportedly relied heavily on Parton to sell records. "All right, Porter Wagner definitely had his own career and he definitely gave Dolly Parton her start in the industry. But Dolly and Porter together were a formidable recording team and I think he definitely relied on her to sell records."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 23 - Women of Country Music in the 70s
facts.name: Porter Wagoner

facts.title: Summer 1967 - Point of No Return
facts.body: A pivotal weekend in the summer of 1967, when Sid Baret went on a five-day excursion with friends involving drugs, is identified as his point of no return. After this event, his sister noted he no longer recognized some people, couldn't remember lyrics, and often fell into catatonic states, remaining motionless for 8-10 hours without blinking. This is believed to be due to severe LSD abuse, marking a permanent change in him. "En ese momento Sid Baret ya cambia para siempre."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.name: Sid Baret

facts.title: Expansion and Famous Locations (1967 - Peak)
facts.body: Seven years after its inception, Tower Records expanded to San Francisco, initiating a rapid growth that eventually led to a peak of 200 locations. Many of these stores were standalone establishments rather than mall-based. Its most renowned location was on the Sunset Strip, at the corner of Sunset Boulevard and Horn Avenue, a popular destination for major stars like Elton John, Michael Jackson, and Bruce Springsteen, known for its exceptional selection of imports and a prominent rooftop billboard promoting new releases. "The most famous location of the mall was on the Sunset Strip, the building at the corner of Sunset Boulevard and Horn Avenue."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of the Record Store
facts.name: Tower Records

facts.title: Atlantic Debut
facts.body: This LP marked Franklin's debut with Atlantic Records and was recorded following her pivotal session at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, and continued at Atlantic's studios in New York City. The album climbed to number two on the Billboard album chart, where it remained for three weeks, positioned between LPs by The Monkees, The Mamas and the Poppas, and Jefferson Airplane. It spent a year and a half on the chart and became her first million-seller, solidifying her status as an album artist at the peak of 60s rock. "Her LP, I Never Loved a Man the Way I Love You, climbed to number two on the Billboard album chart and stayed there three weeks."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Say a Little Prayer Edition Part 1
facts.name: I Never Loved a Man the Way I Love You
